title: "I Will Survive"

canonicalEdition.name: First edition
canonicalEdition.sourceProvenance: Frozen web bundle only: bibliographic records, table-of-contents evidence, official publication metadata, and narrow secondary summary support. Paraphrase-first; no full text frozen.

anchorSummary: Horowitz turns Loudcloud's crisis into a study of survival leadership, where the real work is accepting the severity of the moment and continuing to act before the company runs out of time.
coreClaim: In a collapse, the CEO's first job is not optimism but disciplined survival work: face reality, keep moving, and protect the possibility of another day.
distinctMechanism: Horowitz uses Loudcloud's post-crash danger to show that survival comes from repeated hard calls on financing, communication, and endurance rather than from one dramatic save.
requiredAnchors: Dot-com crash pressure: assumptions about funding and growth stop being reliable.
Cash and existential risk: survival becomes a sequence of decisions under fear and limited options.
Relentless continuation: the title chapter treats persistence as operational discipline, not mood.
specificApplications: Separate useful persistence from wishful thinking in a downturn.
Use cash pressure and runway reality to force sharper prioritization.
Teach that crisis stamina is a decision discipline, not a personality trait alone.
commonMisreadings: Mistaking survival for denial or cheerleading rather than a sober sequence of corrective actions.
Treating persistence as passive endurance instead of active crisis management.
hardEdgeRequirement: Hard mode must show why survival leadership feels psychologically brutal because the CEO has to keep choosing under conditions that rarely reward certainty.
thresholdQuestion: What does disciplined leadership look like when the primary objective is no longer growth but survival?
